# APPROACH TO ENDOCARDITIS

Infectious Diseases and Cardiology consults are essential for proved cases and encouraged for suspected cases. See diagnosis page for more information.

[Diagnosis with Duke Criteria](duke-diagnostic-criteria)

Attempt to identify the pathogen before starting antimicrobials. At least three sets of blood cultures should be obtained from different venipuncture sites.

These cultures should be drawn at different times with the first and last culture separated by at least one hour.

For a patient who is not clinically stable, or if the progression of the illness is rapid, draw 3 sets of blood cultures and then initiate empirical antimicrobial therapy and/or surgical intervention.

Ascertain whether any antimicrobials were taken during the previous 2 weeks to help interpret culture results.

Penicillin susceptibility data are used to determine appropriate antimicrobial therapy for streptococcal endocarditis. Because bacteria in cardiac vegetations are not actively dividing, and are protected from host defense mechanisms, bactericidal antimicrobial regimens are necessary to treat bacterial endocarditis. The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) cut-off levels used to select therapy for endocarditis differ from those used to select therapy for other infectious diseases (see below).

# Penicillin allergy

Beta-lactam antibiotics are more effective than vancomycin for treating susceptible gram-positive pathogens. For patients with penicillin allergy that is known or suspected to be class I (anaphylaxis, angioedema, or hives), penicillin desensitization or therapy with a cephalosporin is usually the best approach.

[Penicillin Desensitization protocol](penicillin-desensitization-protocol)

When gentamicin is used for synergy against gram positive bacteria, serum concentrations should be 3-4 mcg/ml peak and < 1 mcg/ml trough. Once daily gentamicin dosing can be used for streptococcal cases but not for staphylococcal or enterococcal cases.
